https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.title: Climate activists target cars of wealthy
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.text:
Activists deflated the tyres of cars in one of Glasgow’s wealthiest districts as part of direct action against the rich and the “destruction they wreak” on the environment.
Campaigners claim they targeted 60 Range Rovers and other SUV-type vehicles in the city’s West End yesterday morning. Fake notices of police fines were placed on the cars’ windscreens warning owners that their tyres had been let down because of the carbon emissions caused by the vehicles.
The flyers read: “Attention climate violation. Your SUV contributes to the second biggest cause of carbon emissions rise in the last decade. This is why we have disarmed your car by deflating one or more of its tyres.”
However, one resident who discovered her car had been targeted said it was not an SUV, but a two-wheel drive with a 1.6 litre engine.
Lucy Conn, 31, a solicitor, had been planning to drive her three-year-old son to nursery, along with her ten-month-old baby, but had to walk instead. She said tyres on her car and her neighbour’s 1.2 litre model had been punctured.
The protest was carried out by a group calling itself “Tyred of SUVs”, understood to be composed of breakaway activists from Glasgow Calls Out Polluters.
Police arrested 16 of the group’s members this week after they tried to prevent business leaders gathering for a dinner in Glasgow’s Maryhill by blocking the roads and glueing themselves to the doors of the venue.
They cited research from the International Energy Agency, which found the cars were the second largest cause of the global rise in carbon dioxide emissions over the past decade, eclipsing aviation, shipping and trucks.
The group said it apologised if it had accidentally targeted smaller cars.
A spokesman said: “Our intention was to target SUVs only. If Ms Conn’s car was targeted by our group, we apologise.
“The mistake may have been due to the fact that more and more non-SUVs are being designed to look like SUVs — apparently, climate destruction is fashionable.
“We strongly deny damaging car tyres: deflation via the valve is by far the quickest and easiest way to deflate a tyre, and leaves the tyre intact.”
They added: “If the 1 per cent won’t take responsibility for the climate destruction they wreak, we’ll make them.”
A police spokesman said: “We are aware of these incidents and there will be increased patrols in the area to provide reassurance to local residents.”
The latest action came as a group of six Scientist Rebellion activists — a branch of Extinction Rebellion — threw green paint over a Scottish Power building and glued their hands to the ground, in protest at their “greenwashing policies”.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.title: What sort of nimby are you?
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.text:
Forget anger at greenwashing and fishing rights or even the John Lewis Christmas ad — what really unites a divided Britain is far closer to home: planning and housing. Anywhere but in our backyards, unless you can make a profit when you sell the family plot and move far, far away. We all acknowledge that we need to build new houses, but the problem is, no one can agree where to build them.
The backlash against Boris Johnson’s radical proposals to make it easier to build homes — now under review — shows that we remain a nation of nimbys. As those plans are under the microscope we put the different tribes of nimby under the spotlight. Which nimby are you?
Andrew’s grasp of algorithms was shaky enough in the fourth form at St Ethelred’s. Now the self-serving public servant is a backbench Tory MP with 30-odd years’ service for the good people of Little Boring under his rapidly expanding belt. His understanding of how the great Ministry of Levelling Up works out the number of new homes for his patch keeps escaping his brain like thistledown on the wind. Not that there will be much thistledown left round here if that developer — a friend of a really important friend — builds on Bosky Meadow. The Lib Dems are sniffing the wind, so Andrew is vociferously on the side of his anxious flock. Meanwhile, he prays that no one saw anything at the recent Con Club dinner. How was he to know that the developer was a woman?
Daniel (never Danny) did not graduate with a first in architecture from the University of Cambridge, nor spend a year in Baku fetching coffees for the late Zaha Hadid, to have the view from his N16 studio blighted by a new mixed-use scheme so regressive in aspect it would disgrace a chocolate-box lid. Not that he eats chocolate, of course, unless it’s sourced from ethical cocoa beans, and vegan. Furious to the point of tears, he WhatsApps his best pal, Virginia, who agrees that something must be done. She’s an environmental consultant with a doctorate in geothermal energy and a side hustle designing velvet cushions that she sells on Etsy for £90 a pop. Wearing her learning lightly, she’s also a whizz at dealing with the neanderthals on local councils, who stand in awe at her feminine grasp of building regs. Daniel is safe in the knowledge she will fight his battle for him while he stays indoors, googling “Design Review Panel vacancies”.
Peregrine is old, but his lineage is ancient, ramrod straight back to William the Conqueror. His ever-fragrant wife, Penny, was a shop girl when he met her at a florist’s in Belgravia, and she has transformed the gardens at Castle Longshot. Yes, there’s now a profitable tearoom where the old orangery once stood and there are whispers that the man from Ancient Buildings was bought off with six jars of damson jam and a crate of estate chardonnay, but that’s immaterial. What matters is that there is a plan afoot to build social housing in the village, right in the sightline from the top of the tower that houses Peregrine’s dark skies telescope. They won’t stand for it. Meanwhile, since he came back from Dubai, Perry’s heir has been planning to build an entire village as soon as the dear old man pops his clogs.
Caroline is the unofficial leader of the dog walkers’ protest group WOOF (Warning — Off Our Field) because she was a judge at Crufts in 1996 and once met Princess Anne. She has little truck with Extinction Rebellion. Nasty tattoos. With a brace of Welsh terriers and an authoritative way with a whistle, she goes unchallenged by the canines and their humans, who have come together in protest against homes being built on “their” dog-walking field. At the start there had been a few murmurs of dissent led by a local builder with a bull mastiff, but he was soon brought round with a treat. The thing is, no one can find out to whom the field belongs — not even Ian, the local historian. This challenge is buying WOOF time at the developer’s expense and giving the local “newspaper” material as it gleefully stirs the pot.
Jake’s father, a local estate agent, tried to give his only son a job in the family firm, but Jake’s interest in EPCs and best and final offers goes only as far as Karl Marx. “All property is theft,” he reminds his parents as he sallies forth to join his fellow protesters — patron saint, Swampy — from the family home, a sparklingly clean 1930s detached extended to within a millimetre of its boundary. His placard-waving activities are funded by a zero-hours contract in the brewpub on the high street. It’s lost on Jake, but not his parents, that he is still living in his childhood bedroom, with Spider-Man wallpaper, at the age of 24, with no sign of moving out.
Marjorie and Keith have lived in their bungalow since the 1960s, when a builder bought fields off a farmer. The remaining few acres of grassland, populated by bedraggled horses, is their Arcadia, although they lock the doors when the caravans arrive. Definitely Brexiteers, they’ll defend themselves against the levellers with spatulas and spite. They are obsessed with house prices and the probability that the family redoubt will have to be sold to pay for care-home costs, despite what the prime minister says.
Daisy lives in a rapidly gentrifying postcode where her Farrow & Balled Victorian terrace (bought with a bit of Granny’s inheritance) is now worth a tidy sum. Her ex-husband hotfooted it back to London when she dug up the garden for a ground source heat pump. Daisy feels permanently guilty about everything, so she diverts her attention towards all good causes, including the environment. Those 320 edge-of-village houses might be 35 miles away, but it matters, right? Luca and Lulu, her nine-year-old twins, have Uber Eats on speed dial. Daisy’s loud and eloquent voice, courtesy of a good all-girls school, makes her a natural spokeswoman for carbon offset, wildflowers and badgers.
Ian seems like a quiet, unassuming chap until you mention ridge and furrow. He rides a Brompton bicycle and retired early from his job as a geography teacher so he could pursue an MA in the lost railway stations of Norfolk. Since Mother died, he has lived alone in a draughty four-bedroom Edwardian villa with a cat called Philip (after Larkin). He keeps his secret sword of knowledge sheathed close to his chest, which is always zipped up firmly in a sturdy windcheater. Faced by those oleaginous, clipboard-wielding planning chaps from the council, however, he becomes a whirling dervish of righteous anger. His recall of local history is beyond compare and he can always be relied on to dredge up an ancient pinfold to scupper a scheme.
Christine has not spent 40 years working in local government to sit back and watch as the bulldozers roll in, digging up all those municipal flowerbeds to widen the new access road. She is fed up with the mansplaining young pipsqueaks on Zoom, and sick of being patronised by so-called co-workers with fancy degrees and no common sense. Her own modest property portfolio, a buy-to-let that she rents to her favourite nephew and an off-plan ground-floor apartment being prepared for her retirement in Torquay, have given Christine agency. Fortified by HRT (if only she’d known sooner), she’s out for revenge. Naked, if necessary.
Trustafarian Phoebe, who studied art history, and her partner, Mark, whose parents bought their own house under Right to Buy before moving on up the property ladder, are online entrepreneurs. “PJ” and “MJ”, reared on a diet of George Clarke and Kim Kardashian, take themselves terribly seriously because their Insta feed has gained 30,000 followers since they won a magazine competition for giving their kitchen a brushed steel makeover, adding bifold doors and a terrazzo-clad island unit. You’d think such design fiends would welcome new development, but not when that proposed build-to-rent scheme would give its residents a view over their hot tub. MJ is considering taking their case to Good Morning Britain.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/holy-cl.title: Holy climate crisis! Extinction Rebellion’s Christian wing are on a mission to save God’s green earth
https://www.thetimes.com/article/holy-cl.text:
Last week, Justin Welby, the Archbishop of Canterbury, apologised for likening those ignoring the climate crisis to politicians who turned a blind eye to the Nazis in the 1930s. While his outspokenness could be considered an attempt to atone for his previous life as an oil industry executive — he worked in the 1980s for the French oil company Elf Aquitaine in Paris and Enterprise Oil in London — Welby is not the only member of the devout ruffling feathers in the name of saving God’s green earth.
A radical fringe of Christian activists has taken up the battle against climate change as a new mission and has been causing havoc across the country. The direct action is a sharp contrast with the usual view of the (sparsely attended) church in 21st-century Britain, a world of middle-aged women doling out tea and cake, and amiable vicars talking about the leaky roof.
In 2019, Father Martin Newell, a 52-year-old Catholic priest from Birmingham, and Sue Parfitt, a 77-year-old retired Anglican vicar from Bristol, climbed on top of a Docklands Light Railway train in Shadwell, east London, destined for the City. “We are acting to raise the alarm in a spirit of repentance for our complicity in sins against God’s earth and God’s poor,” Newell said.
When the militant climate group Extinction Rebellion (XR) occupied Marble Arch in central London with tents and hammocks the same year, a member of the clergy came to wash the feet of fellow activists. When XR blocked bridges in the capital, Christians chained themselves to vehicles. When they camped in Parliament Square, a Franciscan friar stood in full habit opposite Westminster Abbey, waving the XR flag.
Now XR has its own Christian wing, Christian Climate Action, whose logo combines the ubiquitous XR hourglass and a cross. Members have protests at a Ministry of Defence building near Bristol, helped spray fake blood over the Treasury building in London from a fire engine, landed themselves in the dock for scaling Shell’s London headquarters — and written to Welby criticising him for his lack of support.
More recently, and, for many, more annoyingly, they have joined Insulate Britain in blocking motorways. They also made a four-day walk from Newquay to Carbis Bay, Cornwall, when it hosted the G7 conference this summer.
A fortnight ago, a group of about a hundred Christians arrived in Glasgow on another pilgrimage — “the Camino to Cop26” — from London. Last week, as world leaders yawned in a Glasgow exhibition centre, members of Christian Climate Action staged a “die-in” in the centre of the city, lying across a busy thoroughfare and covering themselves with white cloth.
On a windy morning last month, 71-year-old Tim Hewes, a Church of England priest and Christian Climate Action member from Oxford, glued himself to the front of the building where The Sunday Times’s offices are housed. It was a return visit for Hewes who had, in a previous act of suffering, sewn his lips together in bloody protest.
Caroline Harmon, a 41-year-old carbon literacy trainer from Leicestershire, is among the network’s founders. She says Christian Climate Action was born from the “frustration and desperation” of trying to protect the environment by attending parliament or lobbying MPs. “We just felt like that wasn’t cutting it,” she says. “The first thing Christians were asked to do was to look after the world they’ve been placed in.”
Since getting involved with XR, the group’s unofficial membership has swelled to more than 1,000, with about 150 taking direct action. For them, the climate crisis has sparked a religious revival in the shape of the eco-church and its eco-congregation.
“The phenomenon is one with which most Christian churches will be familiar and will be actively encouraging at the local level,” says David Fergusson, regius professor of divinity at Cambridge.
As worry about climate change intensifies, many churches have put the problem under a theological lens.
“There’s been a reawakening of the doctrine of creation,” Fergusson says, “the sense of human responsibility for creation that one finds in the scriptures, in Genesis chapter one.” It is written in the bible that we are stewards of the earth and of God’s creation, and from this springs a religious duty. At a practical level, alleviating the poverty and inequality that may result from climate change can be considered the frontline work of the church.
That is what drives Val King, a 61-year-old business adviser from Motherwell, Lanarkshire, who took part in the die-in. “It was our way of demonstrating those deaths that have already come and will continue from the war, famine and drought brought about by climate change,” she says.
King had arrived in Glasgow after walking a 25-mile leg of the pilgrimage. As twilight settled on the city, she stood alongside her fellow protestors on the banks of the Clyde. “We will resist the destruction of the planet by following God’s word peacefully,” she announced.
Sally Chapman, 50, a full-time activist, explained how religion had inspired her to protect the planet: “Jesus didn’t hold back when he saw injustice and neither can we.”
Both women have been arrested more than once. King was handcuffed in St Paul’s Cathedral in August after a protest demanding the church stop investing in fossil fuel companies.
It’s not just midlife believers who have heard the call. Another pilgrimage arriving in Glasgow was organised by the Young Christian Climate Network. It had 2,500 Christians aged 18-30 undertaking different legs of a five-month journey from the Cornwall summit in June.
According to the network’s founder, 23-year-old Rachel Mander, the young faithful sought overnight refuge in churches, taking the opportunity to spread the word — that word is now about climate finance and the unsustainable debt into which countries are being plunged as a result of climate change.
For those churches suffering dwindling numbers and a wandering flock, going green might just be the thing that helps engage the Christians of tomorrow. Perhaps it will save us all from eternal damnation too.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/vattenf.title: Vattenfall boss Anna Borg: UK’s nimbys must embrace wind farms
https://www.thetimes.com/article/vattenf.text:
For Anna Borg, visiting Glasgow for Cop26 must feel like stepping on home turf. The chief executive of the Swedish state-owned energy giant Vattenfall, one of Britain’s biggest wind farm developers, has found plenty of support for erecting turbines in Scotland, where it has a number of wind farms.
South of the border, though, it is more of a struggle. Its Vanguard project off the Norfolk coast, which will provide enough electricity to power nearly 2 million homes, has been hit by lengthy delays. The project is nearly 30 miles from the coast — and yet locals are up in arms.
A retired RAF pilot argued that the Norfolk countryside was under threat from plans to construct a network of 40 miles of cables running through land close to his home. He raised £16,000 to challenge the government’s decision to grant development consent to Vattenfall’s project. The High Court this year ruled in his favour, forcing the company back to the drawing board.
“We started out in 2009 to develop these projects — and we’re still waiting for the final consent,” sighs Borg, 50, who warns that Britain is at risk of missing its target of cutting carbon emissions by 68 per cent by 2030 if these projects do not get the go-ahead.
Similar protests have occurred at Vattenfall’s rivals in Britain. Scottish Power’s plans to build two substations in Suffolk faced a backlash from locals including the comedian Griff Rhys Jones.
Treading carefully, Borg, who has been in charge of the power company for just over a year, says people have to make sacrifices to reach net zero. “We need to find some kind of social acceptance for the transformation needed. It’s not possible to make this kind of fundamental transformation without it being noticed. And I think that’s important to acknowledge,” she says of the resistance.
Borg, who has piercing blue eyes and is immaculately dressed, has been making these points to world leaders at Cop26. She believes an overhaul of the planning process must occur if we are to avoid the sort of delays seen in building new nuclear plants. “The trick is to make this happen in reality. And in order to do that, the consulting and the permitting processes need to be smoother and faster.
“It’s a major transition happening in a very short period. So you need a totally different approach to this . . . I think politics play an important role to clear the road of the obstacles.” She wants different steps of the permission process to be run at the same time to speed things up.
It is an argument Borg also made at a dinner last month at Downing Street, in what has been a whirlwind first year in charge. She attended a White House summit on climate change in April, has made the world’s first “green steel” (using hydrogen instead of coal), and brought forward Vattenfall’s deadline for getting to net-zero emissions from 2050 to 2040. The business recently aligned with the Paris climate agreement, meaning it is in line to meet its own goal to help limit global warming to no more than 1.5C.
Borg could easily be a politician herself, carefully navigating questions about the role of protest groups such as Extinction Rebellion — “They are keeping the urgency of the debate . . . but we also need to make this a reality” — while simultaneously backing and rejecting Boris Johnson’s push for developers to source staff and materials from Britain, not abroad: “We prefer to work with local suppliers . . . but there needs to be a mix.”
She was born in Stockholm and her father had a series of managerial roles, while her mother ran her own business. Borg went on to do a master’s degree in economics and political science before becoming a financial services consultant. At the age of 24, she joined Vattenfall, which had focused for decades on hydroelectric power in Sweden, before pushing into nuclear reactors in the 1970s and expanding into Europe.
She worked her way up the company until 2015, when she left to run the Nordic arm of Klarna, the buy-now-pay-later start-up that has become a fintech giant.
Jeanette Anttila, who worked with her at Klarna and is now at Swedish venture capital firm Summa Equity, says Borg adapted well to the vastly different tech start-up culture — even ditching her smart business attire for more casual T-shirt and jeans.
She says Borg had “a laser focus on targets” but was always approachable and friendly: “Some people are really full of themselves, but Anna never uses her power in that way.”
After two years in the job, she was convinced to return to Vattenfall, becoming finance chief in 2017 before taking the top job last year. She now oversees an energy behemoth with 20,000 staff and a turnover last year of £13.7 billion, with pre-tax profits topping £1 billion.
In recent years, Vattenfall has been winding down its coal-fired power stations across Europe, shutting several plants and phasing out the use of lignite coal in Germany — the least efficient type of coal. It has regularly hosted climate protesters at those sites.
Vattenfall owns seven nuclear reactors in Sweden and three in Germany. The German government decided to pull the plug on nuclear in response to the Fukushima disaster in 2011, triggering a huge legal battle with four big operators, including Vattenfall. The Swedish group even dragged the German government before the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington DC, seeking €4.3 billion in damages. This year, it received €1.4 billion (£1.2 billion) in compensation for lost profits on electricity that would have been generated. Those plants are being wound down.
Vattenfall’s attention now is on renewable energy, particularly wind power. Britain is a big focus, Borg says.
Climate sceptics regularly point to the low levels of power produced by wind when there is not much of it, but Borg hits back by claiming better storage solutions in the coming years will fix that: “If you say wind power is not working, what you probably mean is that there is no way to store the electricity produced when there is a lot of wind power.”
BP stunned the industry this year when it teamed up with Germany’s EnBW and splashed out £900 million for a slot in the Irish Sea to build a wind farm — before it even thinks about the cost of developing it. Many observers argued that BP, late to the wind power party, had overpaid in its desperation.
“I think we see a bit of a boom right now because everybody’s sort of running into this space and are also willing to pay high premiums for it,” Borg says. “But of course we will see some projects not being successful as well. You need to know what projects to focus on ... and how to build a profitable wind farm which is cost efficient — because in the end, the customers always pay for the output. And we also don’t want this to be more costly for people than necessary.”
She adds: “If you don’t know enough about what you’re doing, or you pay too much for a project that you’re going to develop, you can easily get lost in the calculations in the sense that it will not be a profitable project in the end. And then we will see projects being closed down.”
Borg is up for the fight as the oil majors try to muscle in on her territory, with her eye on more wind farm sites in Britain for the right price — as long as the nimbys do not get in her way.
Born: February 10, 1971 in StockholmStatus: married with 20-year-old twins (a son and a daughter)Home: StockholmSchool: Kungsgardsskolan high school in NorrkopingUniversity: Uppsala, Sweden — master’s degree in economics and political scienceFirst job: consultant in financial servicesSalary: £670,000 (2020)Car: fully electric Audi e-tronBook: Life 3.0: Being human in the age of artificial intelligence, by Max TegmarkFilm: Hidden FiguresMusic: “Anything that will fill a dance floor or a guitar solo by Brian May [of Queen]”Gadget: the coffee pot on her meeting table in the office. “It has saved many mornings and late afternoons.”Drink: champagne on special occasionsCharity: UnicefLast holiday: Nice, south of France
The chief executive of Vattenfall spends much of her time in meetings — both in person and over video links. Normally, she will make one or two presentations internally or externally, and — when the pandemic subsides — she will travel to different locations and visit the company’s sites.
Borg is very sociable and likes to relax by spending time with friends and family. She also enjoys travelling, keeping fit and reading.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Jeremy Clarkson: If Greta and her pals really want to get results, they should try protesting in Tiananmen Square
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Greta Thunberg is now kayaking back to the Swedish port where she left her bicycle, having spent the week outside a conference centre in Glasgow, swearing a lot and being interviewed by BBC journalists who fawned like they were soap stars being introduced to the Queen. They didn’t call the annoying little bucket of ego, “Your majesty”, but you could see they were thinking it.
I simply don’t get the Thunberg phenomenon. She has no knowledge of how the world works, no manners and no letters after her name because instead of going to school, she’s been busy sailing round the world so she can be mardy and abusive to grown-ups. What she needs is a smacked bottom.
Rod Liddle calls her the “Swedish doom goblin” which is, of course, brilliant, but she’s worse than that. She’s a pest. A 4ft maypole around which the deranged and the weak and the unemployable can dance and chant and make a nuisance of themselves.
However, she did come up with one idea last week that struck a chord. In essence, she said that there was no point listening to whatever the f*** the Cop26 politicians were saying inside their important meetings because the people outside knew what had to be done and could just get on and do it.
Absolutely. I already know that I should not buy palm oil or products that come with unnecessary plastic packaging, and that I should not use wet logs in my wood-burning stoves. I also know that if my journey’s less than a mile, I should walk rather than use the car and that I should make more of an effort to understand what goes in the recycling part of my bin and what doesn’t. I don’t need Joe Biden to wake up from one of his naps and tell me.
So here’s a tip, Greta: lecturing me on what needs to be done is pointless. It’d be like standing in my bedroom every morning ordering me to wear clothes. I know already.
What you should be doing instead is cycling to countries where people are perhaps less well aware of what should be done. China for example. That I’d like to see. Greta standing outside Zhongnanhai with her parka and her Glastonbury backpack and her microphone, lecturing the leaders about their policies on coal and trees and so on. Maybe she could be joined by those Extinction Rebellion halfwits who go to the middle of London to tell Barnes people in Teslas to be more green, rather than going to the slums of Calcutta where two million people, living in poverty, cook their supper every evening on chulha stoves, which blanket the city in a thick yellow fog. These are the people Tarquin and their sexually ambiguous mates should be targeting. But they’re not.
I saw a map, last week, of where the world’s methane is coming from. And let me tell you that billions of tons of the stuff is pouring into the skies from India and China. And not a single hairy person in Liberal Democrat shoes is over there with a placard complaining about it. Because they’re all here, moaning about how my cows burp too much and how there’s a turd in the River Evenlode.
It’s the same story with the loft insulation protesters. There was a photograph in my newspaper on Friday that showed them blocking the path of a lorry that was actually delivering loft insulation. So again, they’re inconveniencing the lives of people who are already doing their best.
They too should be in China because I’d dearly love to see that. Especially the footage of the Chinese police ungluing the hands of a vicar from the tarmac in Tiananmen Square. “Oh no, Reverend. All your skin’s come off.” And now you’ve hit your head on the police car. I’d also like to see them daubing the words “racist” and “murderer” on statues of Chairman Mao, but of course, this would never happen because they know they would not be treated with respect and reverence by China’s news crews. And neither would they be invited with Greta and the Lib Dem vicars round to President Xi’s for some nuclear free vegan peace food.
This is why they’re not protesting in countries where protest might do some good; because they’re timid and wet. Greta turns up in Glasgow so she can bathe in some adulation for a few days, rather than getting sent to a labour camp for a few decades.
That’s what these protesters need to get through their knitted hats and into their thick skulls; that if you want to get something done, and I mean really done, you’ve got to be uncomfortable. And you’ve got to be surrounded by people who don’t like you, not those who do. You’ve got to talk to Fox News, not CNN or the BBC.
Look at Gandhi and Mandela. They were prepared to undergo unimaginable hardships to further the cause in which they believed.
Thich Quang Duc was prepared to go even further. Had this Buddhist monk stepped out of his Austin A95 and glued himself to the road to protest about the South Vietnamese government, it’s virtually certain that no one would remember his name. And I wouldn’t have been able to recall what sort of car he had. But he didn’t glue himself to the road. Instead, he set himself on fire and sat there, in the middle of a busy intersection, until he was dead.
Then you have Emily Davison who, to further women’s rights, leapt under the king’s horse at the Derby and was killed. And the Tolpuddle Martyrs, and William Wallace. I think it’s safe to say that if the blue-faced agitator had fought for Scottish independence by gluing himself to a tree, Mel Gibson would have been less inclined to make that film.
But those days are long gone. Today we have a planet that’s being fried because too many people are living on it. And there’s not a single climate activist who’s prepared to make a protest by reducing the numbers.
